newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Hanbo chief admits political payments.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Hanbo chief admits political payments.

text.p: The founder of South Korea's troubled Hanbo Group, in dramatic testimony broadcast live from a Seoul jail, told a parliamentary inquiry on Monday he had donated money to President Kim Young-sam's election campaign.
The funding of Kim's 1992 campaign is one of the hottest political issues in South Korea.

Hanbo was one of the great corporate success stories under Kim's administration, and the collapse of its steelmaking flagship in January uncovered corrupt links between the group and politicians in both ruling and opposition parties.

Three of Kim's close associates are on trial with Chung and six others in a bribery scandal in connection with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, under debts of $5.8 billion.

Chung told the parliamentary inquiry he contributed up to one billion won ($1.12 million) to the then Democratic Liberal Party through a legitimate channel as a member of the party's financial committee to help fund the 1992 presidential election.
When asked by parlimentarians during a hearing in jail if he made any donation, Chung said: "Yes. As a member of a financial commitee member, I contributed to the election fund."
Asked about the size of the donation, he said: "A political donation is limited to a maximum of one billion won."
The Democratic Liberal Party's name was changed to the New Korea Party after Kim came to power.

Chung, wearing a light blue prison uniform emblazoned with the number 2952, denied giving any money personally to Kim but admitted asking Kim's close associate, Hong In-gil, to help his company obtain bank loans.
Hong, among the 10 people on trial over the scandal, has been charged with accepting bribes from Chung.
Chung also admitted contributing political funds to a group of politicians but declined to give details, saying the issue was pending in his trial.
The hearing in jail, the first in South Korea's history, is being held as part of a 45-day special probe by parliament into the biggest corporate failure in South Korean history.

It was arranged after opposition parties attacked an investigation by state prosecutors into the Hanbo failure as a whitewash that failed to bring to justice major players in the loans-for-kickbacks scandal.
Hanbo Steel's failure revealed a web of corruption and influence-peddling involving top bankers and politicians that allowed the company to secure loans far in excess of its capacity to repay them.
Chung has been charged with using 213.6 billion won of company debt for purposes not related to investment or the operation of Hanbo.
But he denied the charge on Monday, saying all the loans Hanbo obtained were used for the company.
"The misunderstanding arose because of interest payments. About 1.5 trillion won was paid as interest," he said.
Prosecutors, who reopened their probe into the Hanbo scandal last month, said they were probing allegations that senior economic officials were involved in the collapse of Hanbo Steel.
The prosecutors said they were also looking into suspicions that President Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, accepted kickbacks and pressured banks to offer loans to Hanbo.
Opposition members of parliament accused Hyun-chul of accepting a 200 billion won kickback from a businessman acting as an agent for Hanbo.
Kim Hyun-chul is scheduled to testify later this month before the National Assembly's hearing. (Conversion: $1 = 893.6 won)
